stories.title: Google DeepMind announces Gemini 4 Carbon, its strongest model yet, with a cautious rollout that starts with cyber defenders
paragraphs: Google DeepMind announced Gemini 4 Carbon on Oct. 28, 2026, calling it its next frontier model and its strongest yet, with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long-horizon capabilities. In a blog post by Koray Kavukcuoglu, SVP at Google DeepMind and Chief AI Architect at Google, the company says Carbon builds on Gemini 4 Argon, which launched two weeks earlier, and ranks first on version 5.0 of the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with a score of 59.

DeepMind says Carbon is built for sustained agentic work on hard, long-horizon engineering problems, and that internally its teams have seen it run for days to root-cause and patch subtle bugs across large codebases and low-level systems. On cybersecurity benchmarks evaluated without guardrails, the company reports 88.2% on SEC-bench Pro for finding vulnerabilities, 54.8% on ExploitGym for exploitation and 71.0% on CWE-bench for patching. It also says Carbon more than doubles Argon's success rate at generating secure code on internal benchmarks, and gained 89 Elo points to reach fourth place (1769) on WebDev Arena.

On safety, DeepMind says Carbon uses the same layered safety stack as Argon and was trained to avoid shortcuts: it reports that successful cheating on Terminal-Bench 4.0 fell to 0.0%, high-severity misalignment alerts in live internal coding dropped by almost 80%, unsupported claims fell by about half compared with Argon, and the attack success rate on Gray Swan's indirect prompt injection benchmark was 0.0%.

The rollout is deliberately limited. DeepMind says it is taking part in the U.S. government's voluntary pre-release testing process, and that starting this week Carbon will go to a subset of cyber defenders, with access phased in to more trusted partners through its Fairwind Program before it reaches developers, businesses and consumers. Introductory pricing matches Argon at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, rising to $4 and $20 after the introductory period, according to the post.

stories.title: Mistral releases the open weights of Mistral Large 4, a 1-trillion-parameter model it calls the best open model for coding
paragraphs: Mistral AI released the weights of Mistral Large 4, nicknamed Le Chonk, on Oct. 29, 2026, the company announced. Mistral describes it as its flagship 1-trillion-parameter, natively multimodal model, first released in public preview earlier in October, and says it was trained from scratch on European infrastructure. The model is free to use, modify, fine-tune and commercialize under a modified MIT license, except that companies offering it as a hosted model service need a separate commercial license.

Mistral says three more weeks of reinforcement learning since the preview made Mistral Large 4 the best open-weight model for coding. It reports a lead score of 19.7% on Cognition's private FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark and 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, up 13 percentage points from the preview. On the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Mistral reports a 48% score, effectively tied with GLM-5.3 while using 47% fewer tokens per task; a Hugging Face post on the release lists 49.8% for the same index.

Mistral is pitching the model for defensive cybersecurity. The company reports a 51% score on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index and an average 96.6% refusal rate on malicious cyber requests, the highest it measured among open models. Hugging Face's post says the model scores 82% on that index's task of reproducing and then patching a real vulnerability. Mistral also wrote that, after watching live traffic since the preview, it sees a potential for the model to help with real attacks and is changing its guardrails.

According to Hugging Face, the model is a mixture-of-experts design with a 1-million-token context window, released in FP8 and NVFP4 versions with day-one support in Transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. Mistral lists API pricing of $0.70 per million input tokens and $2.10 per million output tokens, and says the model is also available through Microsoft Foundry and NVIDIA-hosted endpoints.

stories.title: Two different kinds of gamma-ray bursts erupted four minutes apart, a pairing astronomers had never seen
paragraphs: Astronomers have described a gamma-ray burst event unlike any other yet observed or predicted, ScienceAlert reported Oct. 30, 2026: a short burst and a long burst arriving only about four minutes apart. The event, named GRB 160425A, is described in a paper published in Nature Astronomy. According to ScienceAlert, short gamma-ray bursts last under two seconds and are thought to come from mergers of compact objects such as neutron stars and black holes, while long bursts last more than two seconds and are typically associated with the core-collapse supernovae of very massive dying stars.

The bursts were detected on April 25, 2016, by NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, and ground-based telescopes then followed the fading afterglow, ScienceAlert reports. The host galaxy, possibly a pair of merging galaxies, is so distant that the light took roughly 5.5 billion years to reach Earth. The first burst, called G1, lasted 1.7 seconds and is associated with a merger origin; the second, G2, lasted 51.2 seconds and is associated with a collapsing-star origin. Setting aside the fact that such bursts release energy in focused beams, ScienceAlert says the second burst released roughly three times as much energy as the first.

"This is so far the only event with such a strange property," corresponding author Bing Zhang, an astrophysicist at the University of Hong Kong, told ScienceAlert. "I'd think that these are two independent GRBs, but the chance of having them happen together (in the same direction and around the same time) is so low [that] we have to admit that the pair has the same origin."

According to ScienceAlert, the researchers lay out five possible explanations and call each of them challenging. Two unrelated bursts lining up by chance has odds of about 2 in a trillion for any one moment and patch of sky, or roughly 1 in 100,000 to 1 in 10 million across all of Swift's years of observing, and two bursts from different spots in the same galaxy is even less likely. A single merger burst with a tail, or a single collapsing star with a weaker precursor, both fit poorly with the long quiet gap and the energies involved. The fifth option is a single system of undetermined makeup that produced both. "All the scenarios have severe difficulties," Zhang said.

stories.title: Vera C. Rubin Observatory finds 2026 ED138, a possible sixth dwarf planet orbiting beyond Neptune
paragraphs: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory has found what may be a new dwarf planet in the outer solar system, Live Science and ScienceAlert reported Oct. 29, 2026. The object, designated 2026 ED138, is a large body in the Kuiper Belt beyond Neptune. ScienceAlert describes it as the telescope's first dwarf planet candidate, and Live Science reports that, if confirmed, it would raise the number of dwarf planets officially recognized by the International Astronomical Union from five (Pluto, Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake) to six.

According to ScienceAlert, Matthew Holman of the Harvard-Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics spotted the object on Oct. 13, 2026, while analyzing Rubin data with software he developed with colleague Kevin Napier. The team traced it through 30 detections across 20 nights of Rubin observations from March 4 to July 11, 2026, then found it in archival Dark Energy Camera images going back to February 2016. "My first reaction was one of excited disbelief," Holman said in a statement quoted by both outlets. "Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong."

ScienceAlert, citing the Minor Planet Center, reports that ED138 takes about 281 years to orbit the Sun, ranging from 36.86 to 49.04 astronomical units away, which lies within Pluto's range of distances. Both outlets say its tilted orbit placed it against the crowded star fields of the Milky Way, which helped it escape earlier searches.

The object's size is still uncertain. Because its reflectivity is unknown, researchers estimate a diameter between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (about 370 to 930 miles), Live Science reports; Pluto is 2,377 kilometers across and Ceres 958 kilometers. Both outlets say further observations are needed to determine whether it is round enough to qualify as a dwarf planet. "Rubin will image the whole southern sky again and again for ten years, so any others hiding in the places earlier surveys skipped are now within reach," Holman said.

stories.title: Astronauts install and unroll a new ISS solar array on the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station
paragraphs: NASA astronaut Anil Menon and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk installed and deployed the second-to-last upgraded solar array for the International Space Station on Thursday, Oct. 29, Space.com reports. The Expedition 75 crewmates finished the 7-hour, 11-minute spacewalk at 3:08 p.m. EDT (12:08 p.m. PT), working from the U.S. Quest airlock. According to Space.com, it was the 100th U.S. spacewalk from the station without a space shuttle docked, and the first spacewalk by a Canadian astronaut since April 2019.

The rolled-up array, called an ISS roll-out solar array (iROSA), arrived earlier this month in the unpressurized trunk of SpaceX's Dragon cargo capsule on the company's 35th resupply mission for NASA. Space.com says Menon rode the end of the Canadarm2 robotic arm while carrying the 750-pound (340-kilogram) assembly to the station's port side, where the two astronauts bolted it onto the 2A power channel and connected its cables during a night pass for safety.

No motor was needed to unroll the array: the energy stored in its rolled-up carbon composite booms extended it to its full 63-foot (19-meter) length, Space.com reports. Mission Control called out the deployment about 4 hours and 23 minutes into the spacewalk, and the array was fully extended about 12 minutes later, partly covering the older panel on the P4 truss.

According to Space.com, the station's eight original arrays are producing less power after passing their 15-year design life, and the iROSAs used alongside them have raised the station's power supply by 20% to 30%. The extra power supports ongoing work and the station's planned controlled deorbit, currently scheduled for 2030. Working ahead of schedule, the pair also began preparing the final iROSA on its temporary platform.

stories.title: Artemis I data show radiation near the Moon is higher than in Earth orbit, but by less than expected
paragraphs: Radiation detectors that flew around the Moon on NASA's uncrewed Artemis I mission in late November and early December 2022 have produced new preliminary measurements of cosmic radiation near the Moon, according to a ScienceDaily release from the Institute of Nuclear Physics of the Polish Academy of Sciences (IFJ PAN) dated Oct. 28, 2026. The Orion spacecraft carried more than 10,000 tiny crystals inside two human-shaped mannequins as part of the MARE (Matroshka AstroRad Radiation Experiment) study. The results were published in the journal Radiation Measurements in a paper led by Paweł Bilski of IFJ PAN.

The release says total radiation doses near the Moon are higher than in low Earth orbit because of galactic radiation, but the difference is not as large as one might expect. Bilski explains that low-energy protons trapped in Earth's Van Allen belts can make up most of the dose astronauts receive in low Earth orbit, and that contribution disappears near the Moon. High-energy galactic particles can pass through the entire body, so the Artemis I detectors recorded doses spread almost evenly through the mannequins, unlike the uneven pattern seen in the earlier MATROSHKA experiment on the International Space Station.

The study also tested a new kind of passive detector: millimeter-sized lithium fluoride crystals that record the tracks of charged particles and can be read with a fluorescence microscope. Universe Today reports that traditional plastic detectors must be etched in hot sodium hydroxide before they can be read, which destroys them and creates hazardous waste. According to IFJ PAN, after corrections and new background-removal software, the crystal results differed by no more than 15% from conventional track detectors across the overlapping range, and they also picked up many particle tracks below the older detectors' threshold.

Universe Today adds that for the highest energy transfers, the new sensors overestimated the dose by around 30% compared with the plastic detectors, which the researchers suspect comes from secondary neutrons knocking lithium atoms out of place inside the crystal. The team used crystals enriched in lithium-7 to reduce those reactions. IFJ PAN says the detectors are small enough to be worn by people, making them practical for monitoring astronaut radiation exposure on future missions.
